newsitem.title: UK: UK shares end sharply lower as banks tumble.
newsitem.headline: UK shares end sharply lower as banks tumble.

text.p: - The UK's FTSE 100 index chalked up its biggest one-day decline in point terms for two months on Monday as bank stocks tumbled and fears grew of a possible rise in UK interest rates later this week.
Worries over the Labour government's first budget, confirmed for July 2, also helped send the index 58.5 points lower at 4,562.8 -- its biggest fall since a 65-point loss on April 1.

With Wall Street unsettled by fresh fears of a rise in interest rates, the FTSE 100 was in near free-fall at one stage late in the session, setting the scene for what analysts and traders said could be a jittery month.

The long-awaited market debut of banking group Halifax dominated trading activity, pompting profit-taking in other financial stocks as investment funds cashed in gains in the sector to finance the purchase of Halifax shares.
Participants noted that other prospective financial flotations could absorb yet more of the cash held by fund management groups.

"The immediate outlook doesn't look so clever, with lots of supply around and with fears about the direction of fiscal and monetary policy," said Richard Kersley, UK strategist at BZW, the investment banking arm of banking group Barclays.

Kersley pointed out that London was the only major European market to close lower, despite growing uncertainties over prospects for European monetary union following the weekend poll victory for the French socialists.

Fresh gains for safe-haven sterling was the last thing UK equities wanted to see, already battered by a succession of profit warnings from top companies whose overseas earnings have been squeezed by the currency's strength.
After reaching the latest of a succession of record highs towards the end of last month, dealers said the FTSE 100 could find if difficult to push higher in the short term.

"The merry-go-round has come to a halt for the time being...maybe the time between now and the end of the month is going to be a bit dull," said one senior dealer. The FTSE last week touched a near-record 4705.2.
UK shares found short-lived support from a rally in continental European markets and for a while the FTSE 100 looked reluctant to break decisively below the 4,600 level

Yet an unsteady performance on Wall Street dragged shares lower towards the close, with the Dow down 25 points as London trading ended and the U.S. Treasury long bond down 4/32 points to yield 6.9 percent.
A stronger-than-expected U.S. purchasing managers' report helped drag U.S. markets lower, renewing fears about the risk of a rise in U.S. interest rates ahead of Friday's key U.S. employment report.

Trading volume in UK equities reached a heavy 1.2 billion shares by 1557 GMT, but about half of that total was in Halifax, as the former building society made its market debut. Halifax shares closed at 735-1/2 in volume of 643 million.
The flotation was the cue for profit-taking in other bank stocks, driven to record highs in recent months as investment funds pumped cash into proxies for the market debutante.
Barclays tumbled 53-1/2p to 11.33-1/2, Abbey National fell 32p to 848-1/2, Lloyds TSB Group shares lost 30-1/2p to 583-1/2 and National Westminster Bank Plc fell 21p to 723-1/2.
Elsewhere, National Power, PowerGen, Mercury Asset Management and Bass were among the biggest losers as they went ex-dividend.
Worries about a hike in UK interest rates loomed as financial markets looked ahead to Friday's Bank of England monetary meeting, the bank's first policy meeting as an independent entity.
"The meeting adds another element of uncertainty and at these levels, market-makers are on the defensive," a dealer said.

Among individual stocks, electrical retailer Dixons recovered from Friday's sharp drop prompted by talk of government action against alleged price controls in the industry. Dixons shares gained 3p to 468.

Insurance broker C.E. Heath jumped 28-1/2p to 130-1/2 on news of a possible management buy-out. CD maker Plasmon rose 15p to 211-1/2 after a positive press comment, while Scottish Media rose 15p to 690 after confirming talks on an agreed bid for Grampian, up 41p at 303-1/2.
-- David Holmes, London Newsroom +44 171 542 5106
